old: This word once named any thin-skinned pocket that swells with fluid, like a blister on skin.
Its Old English ancestor, blǣdre, could mean either 'blister' or the organ we now picture first.
Its Proto-Germanic root, *blēdrǭ, sits behind both the skin-swelling sense and the internal organ we call it today.
clues: This internal organ has a name that, over a thousand years ago in Old English, could just as easily mean a blister on your skin.
The stretchy muscular pouch that stores urine until you need the toilet, holding rather than filtering like the kidneys. Its name long covered any thin-skinned, fluid-filled swelling.
Fish have a swim version that keeps them afloat, the gall version stores bile, and a weak one sends road trippers hunting for rest stops.
